newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Miami centennial turns sour amid scandal.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Miami centennial turns sour amid scandal.

text.p: Just months ago, the citizens of Miami were heralding their city's 100th birthday with a balmy bayfront celebration under palm trees. Now, some are ready to write its epitaph.

With a handful of top politicians facing prison terms, a brigade of fiscal firemen are contemplating something similar to an income tax to shore up Miami's crumbling tax base and avert a state takeover of the city.
Some residents simply want the city to disappear.

A small group of residents plan to start collecting petitions in November calling for the city charter to be revoked and for Miami to be absorbed by the Dade County government. If they get 12,600 signatures, the city would have 120 days to call a referendum.

"What's prompting this is the city's finanical position," said Lou Wechsler, a longtime resident who heads the South Grove Homeowners Association and is helping organise the dissolution campaign. "The graft, the kickbacks -- that's the problem. We've got to get out from under this."
The Miami Herald has run an editorial calling for the city be dissolved and merged into Dade County.
CIVIC PRIDE TURNS TO DISGUST

Miami kicked off its centennial celebration on July 28 with an outdoor party and a series of glowing forecasts for the next hundred years. But the outpouring of civic pride quickly turned to disgust amid a litany of criminal allegations.

City Manager Cesar Odio resigned last month to face federal charges that he demanded kickbacks for a computer contract. Commissioner Miller Dawkins pleaded guilty earlier this month to accepting $100,000 in kickbacks.
Prosecutors said former city finance director Manohar Surana had agreed to plead guilty to related charges and secretly recorded conversations implicating the others.
After the trio resigned, Merrett Stierheim, a highly respected former Dade County manager, was brought in to tackle the mess as interim city manager.
He found a soaring $68 million defict that represents more than 20 percent of the city's operating budget for the year that began on October 1.

"They basically don't have an accounting and budgeting system, an acceptable one," said Milan Dluhy, director of the Institute of Government at Florida International University in Miami. "They borrowed from one restricted account to another just to pay the bills. Some of it is absolutely illegal."
The city is hunting for a top national firm to conduct a complete audit, due in May.

"That's when the veil will fall on Miami, when they see these practices, because the credibility of government is going to get even lower if possible," said Dluhy, who is among the corporate and public finance volunteers recruited by Stierheim to draft a bail-out plan.
Federal officials are already investigating some city bond issues.
POSSIBLE PROBE OF FEDERAL FUNDS
Dluhy predicted the audit would lead to an investigation of Miami's use of federal funds and possibly a state takeover of the city that ranks as the U.S's fourth poorest.
Governor Lawton Chiles could appoint an emergency board to take over city finances if Miami missed a payroll, skipped a bond payment or failed to transfer employee withholding taxes.

The state has never taken over a Florida municipality and at present officials are confident Miami can make the deep cuts needed to bring its budget into line, said Gail Sittig, assistant director of Chiles's Office of Planning and Budget.
Stierheim and his bail-out team are fine-tuning a plan that calls for steep fee and licence increases, service cutbacks, union concessions and the sale of unwanted assets.
But the new fees will raise only a few million dollars and income taxes are constitutionally forbidden in Florida.

The best immediate option is Mayor Joe Carollo's proposed $10 a head monthly tax on workers who commute from outside the city, Dluhy said. The tax, which would be highly unpopular, would boost revenues by $40 million a year but would only be a stopgap.

"The long-term prognosis is quite bad for Miami," Dluhy said. "Miami's been on the slide for years. It's a poor city. The downtown area is not redeveloping like other areas. The middle class left a long time ago. There are still a few wealthy enclaves. Outside of that, I would characterise it as a third world city, with the poverty levels."

A dozen U.S. cities have wrangled with the same middle-class flight and shrinking tax base, Dluhy said. Some, such as Cleveland and Philadelphia, have launched redevelopment campaigns that are slowly bearing fruit.
"It's not something you can do in a year or two," he said. "It will take five years to get the city back on target."
GRAFT ALLEGATIONS MAY DETER BUSINESS

But the criminal charges have exacerbated Miami's problems and could make it difficult to attract new businesses, said Frank Nero, president of the Beacon Council, which promotes economic development.
"Whenever someone is raising the question, "Is this the way business is conducted here?', obviously it's an issue," Nero said.

Miami, whose city commission was famous in the past for paying more attention to Latin American foreign policy than civic matters, has a system of electing commissioners that has prompted allegations of cronyism and nepotism.
That was borne out when one of Stierheim's first actions was to decree that all employees who got their jobs "for reasons other than merit" were officially off the payroll.

But historian Arva Moore Parks, who has chronicled Miami's travails through waves of Indian raids, land grabs, hurricanes, riots and refugee influxes, said the current corruption scandal is hardly Miami's worst.
"There was a very serious crisis in 1937, in what came to be known as the Termite Administration, where voters recalled the entire commission," Parks said.

"It's not without precedent really," she said. "I think it's horrible and I'm very sad about it. But I think there is a community-wide effort to work this thing through. I certainly think we're going to survive it like we've survived everything else."
